summary: HETA combines causal attention-rollout gating, Hessian-based second-order sensitivity, and KL-divergence information loss into a unified attribution framework for decoder-only LLMs, evaluated against a broad baseline suite across four models. The motivation is principled and the experimental breadth is above average, but the evidence is undermined by suspiciously large margins over strong baselines (up to ~6x on Soft-NC) that are never explained, a self-designed metric on a self-authored dataset with circularity risk, and an abstract that claims 'alignment with human annotations' when the labels are actually produced by GPT-4o and GPT-5. The core idea is promising but the evidentiary and calibration issues require substantial revision before acceptance.
strengths: Principled motivation that correctly identifies real limitations of attention- and first-order-gradient attribution in decoder-only autoregressive models, with a coherent three-component design (causal semantic gating, Hessian sensitivity, KL information loss).

Broad baseline comparison (ContextCite, IG, PML, TDD, attention rollout, fAML, Progressive Inference, SEA-CoT, ReAgent) across four decoder-only models of varying scale (3B-70B) and three established benchmarks plus a curated probe.

Comprehensive auxiliary analysis: per-component ablation (six configurations), decoding-hyperparameter robustness sweep, Gaussian-perturbation sensitivity, active/passive syntactic-invariance test, and alignment-F1, which collectively probe stability beyond the main metric.
Causal masking of the attention rollout so attribution mass is restricted to tokens with actual paths to the target is a sensible and well-motivated design choice specific to decoder-only models.

key_concerns.issue: The abstract and Table 1 caption claim 'alignment with human annotations' / 'human-annotated tokens', but the curated-dataset labels are actually generated by GPT-4o and GPT-5 Thinking (intersection at subword level). This is a misrepresentation of the evaluation source and inflates the perceived validity of the DSA and F1-alignment results.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Re-label all references to 'human annotations' as 'automated/LLM-generated annotations' throughout, and either add a genuine human-annotated subset (even small) to validate the GPT-4o/GPT-5 labels or explicitly frame the metric as LLM-alignment rather than human-alignment.

key_concerns.issue: Reported improvements are implausibly large: HETA achieves Soft-NC of 10.3 on LongRA/GPT-J versus ~1.5 for the best baseline, and ~6.4x over ReAgent on LLaMA-3.1-70B (9.9 vs 1.55), while many baselines post negative Soft-NS values. Such margins are extraordinary for interpretability work and are not explained; they raise fairness-of-tuning or metric-implementation concerns.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Provide per-baseline tuning details, confirm identical metric implementations for all methods, include a sanity-check random/uniform-attribution baseline, and explicitly explain mechanistically why HETA's design yields this specific magnitude of gain on Soft-NC/Soft-NS rather than only asserting it.

key_concerns.issue: The DSA metric and the curated dataset are both authored by the same team that designed HETA, and the metric directly rewards concentrating attribution mass on the answer-bearing segment — exactly what HETA's causal gate is built to do. This creates a circularity risk where the method is evaluated on a task structurally biased in its favor.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Have an independent group re-annotate a held-out portion, report DSA for a trivial 'mask-all-but-SciQ-segment' lower bound and an oracle upper bound to contextualize the scores, and validate DSA against an external, non-self-authored attribution benchmark.

key_concerns.issue: Theoretical justification (error bounds, Hutchinson-estimator convergence, justification for the multiplicative gating and the β=γ=0.5 weighting) is relegated to appendices that are not in the main text; the body gives no argument for why this particular combination or these weights are principled rather than tuned.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Move the key error bound and the justification for the combination form into the main method section, and report a β/γ sensitivity sweep showing the score is not critically dependent on the 0.5/0.5 choice.

key_concerns.issue: Compute cost is acknowledged qualitatively ('higher runtime, greater memory') but never quantified against baselines in the main text, while HETA uses Hessian-vector products that are far more expensive than gradient/attention baselines. Without a cost-vs-quality comparison the practical contribution is unclear, and baselines may be disadvantaged on a fixed budget.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Add a table of wall-clock time and peak memory per attribution for HETA (full and LR+WIN variants) versus each baseline, and discuss baselines' performance under matched compute (e.g., more ablation samples for ContextCite).

key_concerns.issue: Equation (5) is ambiguous: it is unclear whether MT[i] multiplies both (βS+γI) or only the Hessian term, and the normalization constant Z in the semantic-transition formula is malformed in the extraction.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Re-state equation (5) with explicit parentheses and clarify the gating scope; verify all inline equations render correctly.

key_concerns.issue: ReAgent is cited in the text as the 'next best method' on GPT-J but is absent from the GPT-J and Phi-3 rows of Table 3, creating an inconsistency between prose and table.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Add ReAgent rows for all model blocks in Table 3, or clarify which table the 'next best' comparison refers to.

key_concerns.issue: Only three random seeds are used and no significance tests are reported; while the large margins make significance plausible, the 'std < 0.2' / 'std < ±0.06' reporting is thin for the robustness and decoding-sweep claims.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Increase to at least 5 seeds for the main table and report paired significance tests (or bootstrap CIs) for HETA vs ReAgent and SEA-CoT.

questions_for_authors: Why is HETA's Soft-NC improvement over the best baseline (~6x) so much larger than is typical for attribution methods? Could the baselines be mis-tuned or the metric computed non-uniformly across methods?

The curated-dataset labels are generated by GPT-4o and GPT-5; what evidence supports treating these as ground-truth 'human' annotations, and how sensitive are DSA/F1 results to the choice of annotator model?
How were β=0.5 and γ=0.5 selected, and how does HETA perform across a grid of (β, γ) values? Is the method robust to these weights or were they tuned on the test data?
What is the wall-clock and memory cost of HETA (full and LR+WIN) relative to each baseline, and how do baselines perform if given a compute budget matched to HETA's?

Given the DSA metric rewards mass on the answer-bearing segment, what is the DSA score of a trivial baseline that attributes uniformly within the SciQ segment, and of an oracle that attributes only to the gold answer span?

Are the theoretical error bounds in Appendix A2 for the Hutchinson Hessian estimator, the semantic-transition approximation, or the combined score, and do they hold under the low-rank + windowing variant actually used in the main experiments?
calibration_check: Claims are over-scoped: the abstract's 'alignment with human annotations' is unsupported (labels are LLM-generated), 'new standard for interpretability' overclaims given the unexplained margins and circular evaluation, and the SOTA framing is not warranted without addressing the fairness and compute-matching concerns.

significance.justification: LLM attribution is an important subfield and a unified causal+curvature+information framework is useful, but the contribution is a combination of existing ideas and its impact depends on results whose credibility is in question.

novelty.justification: Each component (attention rollout, Hessian sensitivity, KL masking) is established; the novelty lies in their combination with causal gating for decoder-only models, which is incremental rather than fundamentally new.

rigor.justification: The method is plausible but the claim-evidence link is weakened by unexplained implausible margins, a self-designed metric/dataset with circularity risk, and theory relegated to an appendix not visible in the main text.

statistical_soundness.justification: Only three seeds, no significance tests, and thin variance reporting; the huge reported gaps paradoxically make the absence of rigorous significance testing and fairness controls more concerning rather than less.

calibration_honesty.justification: The abstract claims 'human annotations' that are actually GPT-4o/GPT-5 labels, asserts a 'new standard' and SOTA without compute-matching, and buries the main limitations (cost, circularity) briefly in the conclusion.

clarity.justification: The narrative is readable and well-motivated, but equation (5) is ambiguous about the gating scope, several inline equations are malformed, and the relationship between the three components could be stated more precisely.

structure_compliance.justification: Standard sections (Introduction, Motivation, Background, Method, Experiments, Related Work, Conclusion) are present and reasonably organized within a normal conference length.

reproducibility.justification: Models, key hyperparameters (β, γ, rank, window, batch), and dataset construction are described, but the Hutchinson sample count m and several cost details are only referenced as 'reported in experiments' without visible values; code/data availability is stated but anonymized.

related_work.justification: Prior attribution methods (ContextCite, TDD, PML, ReAgent, IG, attention rollout) are discussed with fair characterizations of their limitations, and positioning against them is reasonable and current.

figure_quality.justification: Captions describe informative comparisons (ablation bars, sensitivity/robustness/F1, decoding-sweep table, qualitative attribution maps), but without rendered figures the design quality cannot be judged and the qualitative examples (Figs 2d, 3d) are only weakly described.

breadth_generality.justification: Four models and three benchmarks plus a curated probe give surface breadth, but generality is under-supported because the curated metric is self-designed and potentially circular, the largest gains are on a single metric, and compute-matched baselines are missing.

overall_recommendation.justification: A promising and broadly-evaluated framework that is not acceptable as-is due to blocking calibration issues (false 'human annotation' claim), unexplained implausible margins, and circular self-evaluation; substantial revision is required.
